title: CAN A GENUINE CHRISTIAN LIVE IN UNREPENTANT SIN FOR YEARS? THE ANSWER MAY TERRIFY THOSE WHO FEEL SAFE—AND BRING HOPE TO THOSE WHO ARE BROKEN.
paragraphs: CAN A GENUINE CHRISTIAN LIVE IN UNREPENTANT SIN FOR YEARS? THE ANSWER MAY TERRIFY THOSE WHO FEEL SAFE—AND BRING HOPE TO THOSE WHO ARE BROKEN.

What if the greatest danger to your soul is not the sin you are struggling to overcome, but the sin you have learned to defend? And what if the very conviction you are trying to silence is evidence that God is still calling you home?
There is a kind of silence that happens when a person reads a Bible verse and suddenly realizes the verse is reading them.
Not their neighbor.
Not their spouse.
Not the hypocrite at church.
Them.
Perhaps you know that silence.

You are sitting alone, scrolling through your phone, when something about Jesus appears on your screen. You almost keep scrolling. You have responsibilities, problems, messages waiting, bills to pay, and a thousand reasons not to think too deeply about eternity.
But something makes you stop.
And suddenly, a question you have avoided for years rises from somewhere deep inside your heart.
“What if I have been calling myself a Christian while refusing to surrender the very thing Jesus has been asking me to leave behind?”
That question is uncomfortable.
It should be.
Because there is a difference between a believer who falls into sin and a person who has made peace with sin.
There is a difference between someone who hates the chains around their wrists and someone who has started decorating those chains.
And there is a difference between trusting the grace of Jesus Christ and using the language of grace to excuse rebellion against Him.
The question is not whether a genuine Christian can sin.
Scripture settles that immediately.
The question is far more serious.
Can someone truly belong to Jesus Christ, remain knowingly and defiantly unrepentant for years, and still confidently claim that nothing is wrong with their relationship with God?
Before answering, we need to walk into a moment from the life of Jesus.
Because the answer is not found in how religious we appear.
It is found in who Jesus is, what He saves us from, and what His grace actually does to a human heart.
Imagine a courtyard in Jerusalem.
The morning air is cool. Dust rises beneath hurried footsteps. Religious leaders have gathered around a woman whose private sin has become a public spectacle.
She has been caught in adultery.
Her reputation is collapsing in front of strangers.
There is nowhere to hide.
The men standing around her are holding something more dangerous than accusations.
They are holding stones.
And standing before them is Jesus.

In John 8:1–11, a passage whose manuscript history deserves careful attention because it is absent from some of the earliest surviving manuscripts of John, the familiar account reaches its unforgettable conclusion.
Jesus says:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11, KJV
The traditional Greek text records His command:
πορεύου, καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε
Poreuou, kai apo tou nyn mēketi hamartane.
“Go, and from now on sin no more.”
Notice what Jesus does not say.
He does not say, “Your sin never mattered.”
He does not say, “Continue living however you want.”
He does not say, “Since I have shown you mercy, obedience is unnecessary.”
But neither does He join the crowd in destroying her.
He extends mercy.
And then He calls her into a different life.
That is the beauty of the Gospel.
Jesus does not offer forgiveness because sin is harmless.
He offers forgiveness because sin is deadly, and sinners cannot rescue themselves.
Grace does not pretend the prison is a palace.
Grace opens the prison door.
And repentance means we stop insisting that captivity is freedom.

Now imagine that woman returning to the same destructive life, defending the same choices, rejecting every warning, and announcing that Jesus had approved of everything because He had refused to condemn her.
Would that be a faithful understanding of His mercy?
Of course not.
Yet this is precisely the misunderstanding that has quietly entered many modern conversations about Christianity.
We have sometimes reduced salvation to a sentence spoken years ago.
A prayer at an altar.
A baptism certificate.
A childhood memory.
A raised hand during a worship service.
A social media biography that says “Follower of Christ.”
Those things may be connected to genuine faith.
But none of them can replace genuine faith.
You can remember the day you walked down a church aisle and still need to ask whether you are walking with Christ today.
You can know the language of worship without surrendering the direction of your life.
You can sing about the cross while protecting the very rebellion that nailed your Savior there.
And that is why the apostle John wrote words that should make every professing Christian examine their heart.
“Whosoever abideth in him sinneth not: whosoever sinneth hath not seen him, neither known him.” — 1 John 3:6, KJV
Read that carefully.
Because if we misunderstand it, we will either crush struggling believers with despair or comfort unrepentant sinners with false assurance.
The Greek text says:
πᾶς ὁ ἐν αὐτῷ μένων οὐχ ἁμαρτάνει
Pas ho en autō menōn ouch hamartanei.
A close rendering is:
“Everyone who abides in Him does not sin.”
The word μένων (menōn) comes from menō, meaning to remain, continue, or abide.
The word ἁμαρτάνει (hamartanei) comes from hamartanō, meaning to sin.

John uses present-tense language, which, together with the surrounding argument, points to the incompatibility between abiding in Christ and a life characterized by sin. We must be careful, however: Greek present tense alone does not automatically mean “continually” or “habitually.” The context, not a grammatical shortcut, guides our interpretation.
And that context is crucial.
Because earlier in the same letter, John says:
“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” — 1 John 1:8, KJV
He also writes:
John is not contradicting himself.
He is confronting two different lies.
The first lie says, “A real Christian never sins.”
The second says, “A real Christian can embrace sin without concern.”
Both are spiritually dangerous.
The Christian life is not sinless perfection.
But neither is it comfortable surrender to sin.
A genuine believer may fall terribly.
A genuine believer may struggle with the same temptation for years.
A genuine believer may experience seasons of spiritual coldness, confusion, disobedience, and even grievous failure.
But Scripture never encourages someone to treat settled, defended, unrepentant sin as harmless evidence of a healthy relationship with Christ.
The presence of a struggle does not prove the absence of salvation. But the absence of repentance should never be treated as proof of its presence.
Think about Peter.
He walked with Jesus.
He witnessed miracles.
He heard teachings that generations of believers would later treasure.
And when the pressure became unbearable, he denied knowing the Lord.
Not once.
Three times.
Imagine the sound of that rooster.
Imagine the memory of Peter's own voice.
“I know not the man.” — Matthew 26:74, KJV
And then Luke records that Jesus turned and looked at Peter.
What followed was devastating.
“And Peter went out, and wept bitterly.” — Luke 22:62, KJV
He had failed the One he loved.
But his failure was not the end of his story.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored Peter, as recorded in John 21:15–19.
Peter's tears did not purchase forgiveness.
Christ's mercy was not earned by emotional intensity.
But his grief belonged to the story of a man who could no longer pretend that his denial was acceptable.
Now compare that with Judas.
Judas also followed Jesus outwardly.
He also heard His teachings.
He also lived among the disciples.
He even expressed remorse after betraying Christ.
Yet Matthew 27:3–5 tells us that his remorse ended in tragedy.
The contrast must not be oversimplified. Peter's tears were not a magic formula, and Judas's story is not a reason to despair over anyone who has sinned terribly.
But together their stories force us to consider a vital distinction.
Feeling bad about consequences is not necessarily the same as turning toward God.
The apostle Paul writes:
The Greek word for repentance is μετάνοια (metanoia).
It refers to repentance, a change of mind and heart that involves turning away from sin and toward God.
It is more than feeling embarrassed.
More than fearing exposure.
More than crying because someone discovered what you did.
Biblical repentance is a genuine turning toward God that bears fruit in changed attitudes and actions.
That does not mean the struggle instantly disappears.
It means sin is no longer something you want to enthrone as your master.
Consider the person who has been battling pornography for years.
They hate what it is doing to their mind, their marriage, their integrity, and their communion with God.
They confess. They seek help. They establish boundaries. They sometimes fall again, and each fall brings renewed grief and a desire to return to Christ.
They need the Gospel, wise discipleship, accountability, and perhaps professional help for deeply entrenched patterns.
Now consider another person who indulges the same sin, refuses correction, deliberately hides it, justifies it, and says, “God understands. I am saved by grace. Nobody can tell me how to live.”
The outward sin may look similar.
But the heart's posture toward that sin is profoundly different.
We cannot see either person's heart perfectly.
Only God can.
But Scripture gives us no permission to reassure the second person that deliberate rebellion is spiritually safe.
And the same principle applies beyond sexual sin.
A husband may quote Bible verses every Sunday while emotionally terrorizing his wife throughout the week.
A business owner may donate generously to ministry while deliberately cheating employees.
A church leader may preach repentance publicly while exploiting people privately.
A believer may maintain a polished Christian image while nurturing bitterness, racism, cruelty, greed, dishonesty, or unforgiveness.
And perhaps the most frightening part is how easily we can become skilled at explaining away what we refuse to surrender.
We stop calling it pride.
We call it confidence.
We stop calling it greed.
We call it ambition.
We stop calling it gossip.
We call it concern.
We stop calling it bitterness.
We call it protecting our peace.
We stop calling it lust.
We call it human nature.
We stop calling it rebellion.
We call it freedom.
Until one day, we have constructed a version of Christianity in which Jesus is welcome as Savior but unwelcome as Lord.
And then the words of Jesus confront us.
“And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?” — Luke 6:46, KJV
That question is not aimed only at the obviously immoral.
It reaches the respectable.
The religious.
The churchgoing.
The generous.
The person who knows all the correct answers but has quietly stopped allowing those answers to correct their life.
Jesus also warned:
“Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven.” — Matthew 7:21, KJV
Those are among the most sobering words in Scripture.
Not because Jesus delights in terrifying wounded people.
But because false assurance is a terrible thing.
A doctor who discovers a dangerous illness does not demonstrate compassion by hiding the diagnosis.
Love tells the truth.
And the truth is that a profession of faith without a corresponding life of repentance deserves serious examination.
Yet here is where we must be extraordinarily careful.
We must never confuse salvation by grace with salvation earned by moral performance.
The Gospel does not say that God accepts us because we have finally become sufficiently obedient.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares that we are saved by grace through faith, not by our works.
Then verse 10 says we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
The order matters.
We do not obey in order to purchase salvation.
We are called to obey because God's saving grace creates a new relationship with Him.
Good works are the fruit of salvation, not the price of admission.
Paul says something astonishing in Romans 6.
“What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid.” — Romans 6:1–2, KJV
The Greek response is:
μὴ γένοιτο
Mē genoito.
An emphatic rejection often translated “By no means!”
Paul anticipated the argument that if grace increases where sin increases, perhaps Christians should simply keep sinning.
He rejects it decisively.
Why?
Because union with Christ changes our relationship to sin.
The Christian is not merely someone who has received a heavenly exemption from punishment.
The Christian is someone who belongs to the crucified and risen Savior.
And belonging to Jesus means that sin no longer has a rightful claim to rule our lives.
Not because we are strong enough.
But because Christ is alive.
Because the Holy Spirit works within His people.
Because grace does more than pardon.
Grace teaches.
Titus 2:11–12 describes the grace of God as teaching us to deny ungodliness and worldly desires and to live godly lives.
Grace is not God's permission slip for spiritual destruction.
Grace is God's undeserved favor bringing us into a new life.
And that raises the question many people are afraid to ask.
What about someone who has lived in unrepentant sin for ten years?
Twenty years?
An entire adult lifetime?
Can that person still be a genuine Christian?
The most biblically responsible answer requires both seriousness and humility.
Scripture does not give us a precise number of months or years after which we can infallibly declare that someone was never saved.
God alone knows the heart.
Christians also differ in how they understand the relationship between perseverance, assurance, and the possibility of falling away.

Many Reformed and other perseverance-oriented Christians understand prolonged, final unrepentance as evidence that a person's profession of faith was never genuine, drawing on passages such as 1 John 2:19.

Many Wesleyan, Arminian, and other Christian traditions warn that a genuine believer can turn away from faith through persistent, willful rebellion, drawing on warnings such as Hebrews 3:12–14 and Hebrews 10:26–29.
Those are meaningful theological differences.
But neither perspective makes comfortable, defiant, unrepentant sin something to celebrate.
And neither should be used to issue a confident final verdict about a particular person's eternal destiny.
The practical biblical warning remains urgent.
If you have spent years refusing God's correction, do not use a past religious experience to silence the warnings of Scripture.
Do not say, “I prayed the prayer, so nothing else matters.”
Do not say, “I was baptized, so I can live however I choose.”
Do not say, “Once saved, always saved,” as though a theological phrase were permission to disregard Jesus.
And do not assume that because God has not immediately exposed or disciplined you, He has approved your behavior.
Romans 2:4 asks whether we despise the riches of God's goodness, forbearance, and longsuffering, not knowing that His goodness leads us to repentance.
Sometimes what we interpret as permission is actually patience.
And patience should never be mistaken for indifference.
Picture a father standing at the doorway of his home late at night.
His child has wandered into danger.
The father keeps the porch light burning.
He watches the road.
He longs for his child to return.
The light is not an endorsement of the dangerous road.
It is an invitation to come home.
And this is where the story of the prodigal son becomes almost unbearable in its beauty.
In Luke 15, a younger son demands his inheritance, leaves his father's house, and wastes everything.
He exchanges belonging for independence.
Security for pleasure.
Home for a distant country.
And eventually he finds himself hungry, humiliated, and desperate.
Then Scripture says:
“And when he came to himself...” — Luke 15:17, KJV
What a remarkable phrase.
He came to himself.
Sin had promised him freedom but had left him barely recognizing the person he had become.
And perhaps someone reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You remember when prayer came naturally.
You remember when worship could bring tears to your eyes.
You remember when your conscience was tender.
You remember when the thought of disappointing Jesus actually grieved you.
But somewhere along the way, compromise became routine.
One secret became another.
One excuse became a lifestyle.
And what once disturbed you now barely registers.
You still believe in God.
You still know the songs.
You might even be serving in church.
But privately, you know there is something you have been refusing to bring into the light.
Perhaps nobody else knows.
Perhaps everybody thinks you are spiritually strong.
Perhaps the people who admire your faith would be shocked to discover the things you have learned to conceal.
And the worst part is not simply the secret.
It is the exhaustion of maintaining two versions of yourself.
One for Sunday.
One for the rest of the week.
One for public worship.
One for private indulgence.
One who talks about holiness.
One who keeps negotiating with temptation.
You have become tired of hiding.
But you are terrified of being found out.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not call you to continue pretending.
It calls you to Jesus.
The prodigal son did not return home with a presentation explaining why his rebellion had been reasonable.
He came back acknowledging his sin.
And before he could finish his prepared speech, his father welcomed him.
Luke 15:20 says the father saw him while he was still a great way off, had compassion, ran, embraced him, and kissed him.
That is not a picture of sin being declared harmless.
It is a picture of mercy welcoming a repentant sinner.
The son returned from rebellion.
The father responded with compassion.
And the celebration was not because the son had successfully defended his sinful choices.
It was because the lost had been found.
The dead was alive again.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Not that your past never happened.
Not that your choices have no consequences.
Not that repentance magically repairs every wounded relationship overnight.
But that through Jesus Christ, forgiveness and new life are genuinely offered to sinners who cannot save themselves.
And there is something even more powerful than the story of a father running toward his returning son.
There is the historical reality of the Son of God going to a cross for sinners.
Jesus Christ lived without sin.
He was betrayed, condemned, mocked, beaten, and crucified.
He bore our sins, as 1 Peter 2:24 declares.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again on the third day, according to the Scriptures.
The cross tells us two things that must never be separated.
Our sin is more serious than we want to admit.
And God's mercy in Christ is greater than we could ever deserve.
Look at the cross before you call sin harmless.
Look at the empty tomb before you call yourself hopeless.
The Savior who died for sinners did not remain in the grave.
And that means the person you have become does not have to be the person you remain.
But we must also talk about a passage that has frightened many sincere believers.
Hebrews 10:26 says:
“For if we sin wilfully after that we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remaineth no more sacrifice for sins.”
Those words deserve reverence, not careless interpretation.
The surrounding passage warns against a deliberate rejection of Christ and His sacrifice after receiving knowledge of the truth.
It is not teaching that every Christian who knowingly commits a sin has automatically passed beyond forgiveness.
If that were the meaning, Peter's restoration, the call to confession in 1 John 1:9, and the many biblical appeals to repent would become difficult to reconcile.
The warning is about something profoundly serious: treating the sacrifice of Christ with contempt and turning away from the only Savior who can cleanse us.
There is no alternative sacrifice waiting somewhere beyond Jesus.
No second Messiah.
No better cross.
No other Savior.
That is why deliberate rejection of Him is so dangerous.
And that is also why the answer to spiritual fear is not to run farther away.
It is to turn toward Him.
If you are frightened because you have sinned, the answer is not to declare yourself permanently abandoned.
If you are grieving because you have wandered, the answer is not to surrender to despair.
If you are asking whether you can still come back, hear the invitation of Jesus:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37, KJV
What a promise.
Not “I will receive only those who have never failed.”
Not “I will welcome only those who can prove they will never struggle again.”
But the one who comes to Him will not be cast out.
And yet coming to Jesus cannot honestly mean demanding that He leave our rebellion untouched.
We cannot cling to the Savior while insisting that our sin must remain our master.
Repentance is not a payment offered in exchange for forgiveness.
It is the fitting response of faith to the mercy of God.
It is turning away from the lies that have been destroying us and turning toward the One who gives life.
And sometimes repentance is not dramatic.
Sometimes it looks like a trembling confession whispered in a dark bedroom.
Sometimes it looks like deleting the secret account.
Sometimes it looks like telling the truth after years of dishonesty.
Sometimes it looks like returning stolen money.
Sometimes it looks like asking for help with an addiction you can no longer manage alone.
Sometimes it looks like confessing a hidden pattern to a mature, trustworthy believer.
Sometimes it looks like accepting church discipline instead of attacking everyone who confronts you.
Sometimes it means leaving an abusive or exploitative situation safely, seeking protection, and refusing to confuse forgiveness with remaining exposed to harm.
And sometimes repentance begins with the smallest, most difficult sentence a proud human heart can speak.
“Lord, I was wrong.”
Not “Lord, they made me do it.”
Not “Lord, everyone else is doing it.”
Not “Lord, You know how difficult my life has been, so my behavior should not matter.”
Just the truth.
“Lord, I have sinned. Have mercy on me.”
And if that prayer is genuine, do not despise its small beginning.
A bruised reed He will not break, as Matthew 12:20 teaches.
But neither should we confuse the beginning of repentance with permission to avoid its fruit.
Real repentance seeks change.
It receives correction.
It makes restitution where appropriate.
It pursues reconciliation where possible and safe.
It seeks accountability.
And it keeps coming back to the grace of Christ, not as an excuse to remain enslaved but as the only hope of freedom.
There is another distinction that matters deeply.
A believer struggling against sin may experience repeated failures without being characterized by settled, unrepentant rebellion.
Duration alone does not tell the whole story.
Someone may spend years battling an entrenched sinful habit while sincerely seeking Christ, receiving help, and learning to walk in obedience.
Someone else may commit fewer outwardly visible sins while harboring a proud, hardened refusal to repent.
God sees what human observers cannot.
This is why we must be slow to pronounce eternal judgments over other people and quick to examine ourselves.
Paul writes:
Notice the invitation.
Examine yourselves.
Not obsessively measure every emotional fluctuation until you lose all peace.
Not make your spiritual confidence depend on perfect performance.
Not compare yourself with someone whose struggles are different.
Examine whether your confidence is rooted in the real Christ of Scripture and whether your life shows the transforming work of His grace.
Ask yourself whether you are bringing your sin into the light or constructing better hiding places.
Ask whether you receive biblical correction or immediately attack the messenger.
Ask whether you desire holiness, even when you stumble.
Ask whether your view of grace makes you love Jesus more or simply makes disobedience easier to justify.
And above all, ask whether you are trusting in Jesus Christ Himself or merely in the memory of something religious you once did.
Because one day, every earthly title will fall silent.
Pastor.
Deacon.
Worship leader.
Ministry founder.
Church member.
Christian content creator.
Longtime believer.
None of those labels can take the place of knowing Christ.
And none of those labels can make unrepentant rebellion spiritually safe.
There is no amount of religious visibility that can compensate for a heart determined to remain hidden from God.
But here is the beautiful interruption of grace.
You are reading this now.
Not yesterday.
Not after another decade of excuses.
Now.
And the call of Scripture is not to wait until you feel sufficiently worthy.
It is to respond to God today.
Hebrews 3:15 says:
“To day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts.”
Perhaps that is the sentence you needed.
Not another argument.
Not another explanation of why your situation is complicated.
Not another promise to change someday.
Today.
Because every time we justify what God calls us to forsake, we practice resisting the truth.
And every time we surrender to Christ, we acknowledge that His wisdom is greater than our excuses.
This is not about earning a place in heaven through sheer willpower.
It is about the living Savior who calls sinners to Himself and transforms them by His grace.
The same Jesus who restored Peter.
The same Jesus who received tax collectors and sinners.
The same Jesus who spoke truth to the rich young ruler.
The same Jesus who told people to repent and believe the Gospel.
The same Jesus who promised rest to the weary.
The same Jesus who died for the ungodly.
The same Jesus who rose victorious over death.
He has not changed.
His holiness has not diminished.
His mercy has not expired.
His invitation is not empty.
And His grace is not powerless.
If you have been hiding behind religious activity, come into the light.
If you have been using grace as permission to sin, stop misrepresenting the gift that cost Christ His blood.
If you have been crushed by repeated failure while sincerely longing to obey Him, do not mistake your battle for proof that He has abandoned you.
If you have harmed someone, take responsibility and seek to make things right without demanding immediate forgiveness or trust.
If you have wandered far, do not spend another year rehearsing why you cannot return.
Come to Jesus.
You may need pastoral care.
You may need trusted Christian accountability.
You may need professional support for addiction, trauma, or destructive behavioral patterns.
You may need to confess something that will have real consequences.
Following Christ does not guarantee that every earthly consequence disappears.
But no consequence makes His grace less precious.
And no genuine act of repentance is wasted.
Perhaps right now, you are asking the question with which we began.
Can a genuine Christian live in unrepentant sin for years?
Here is what you must not miss.
Scripture does not authorize us to determine a person's eternal state merely by counting the years of their failure.
But it also does not authorize us to offer comfortable assurance to someone who persistently, knowingly, and defiantly rejects repentance.
A Christian can fall.
A Christian can struggle.
A Christian can experience grievous seasons of disobedience.
But a life settled in rebellion is a grave spiritual warning, not a condition to be casually explained away.
And if that warning exposes something in your heart, the answer is not to manufacture enough fear to change yourself.
The answer is to bring your whole life to Jesus Christ.
Because the purpose of biblical conviction is not merely to make you feel terrible.
It is to call you away from sin and toward the Savior.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — KJV
And Romans 8 continues by describing the Spirit's work in those who belong to Christ.
Freedom from condemnation is not freedom to worship sin.
It is freedom to belong to Jesus.
And perhaps the most astonishing thing about this entire question is that Christ already knows the truth about you.
Every hidden compromise.
Every failed promise.
Every excuse.
Every tear.
Every secret you have worked so hard to keep.
Nothing surprises Him.
Yet the Gospel still announces forgiveness and new life through His death and resurrection.
Not because your sin is small.
But because His saving work is sufficient.
Not because you deserve another chance.
But because grace is undeserved.
Not because transformation is easy.
But because the risen Christ is mighty to save.
So stop asking only how much sin a Christian can get away with.
Start asking what it means to belong to the One who loved you and gave Himself for you.
Stop measuring the boundaries of permissible rebellion.
Start looking at the beauty of holiness.
Stop treating repentance as a threat to your happiness.
Start recognizing that the sin you defend may be the very thing destroying the joy you are desperate to recover.
And when you fall, do not build a house where you fell.
Confess.
Seek help.
Get up.
Return to Christ.
Walk in the light.
Again and again, depend on His grace.
Not because repentance makes you your own savior.
But because Jesus is the Savior, and His people are called to follow Him.
If this message has uncovered something you have been afraid to acknowledge, you do not need to expose private details publicly. But perhaps you can take one honest step today.
You do not owe strangers your secrets to prove that your repentance is real.

And if this has reminded you of God's faithfulness through your own failures, consider sharing a brief testimony. Someone who believes they have wandered too far may need to hear that the grace of Jesus Christ is not exhausted.
There may be someone on your Facebook friends list who has stopped attending church because shame convinced them they could never return.
Someone who still quotes Scripture but has secretly surrendered to a destructive habit.
Someone who thinks Christianity is nothing but condemnation.
Someone who believes that grace means they never need to change.
Someone who is one honest prayer away from beginning a difficult journey home.
Not to embarrass anyone.
Not to prove how righteous you are.
But because biblical truth, spoken with compassion, can reach places our personal conversations sometimes cannot.
There is also something deeply meaningful about helping make resources like these available to more people.
These resources are intended to help people study Scripture, strengthen their understanding of the Gospel, develop consistent devotional habits, and grow in spiritual maturity.
We glorify God by trusting Christ, obeying His Word, loving others, serving faithfully, and giving willingly according to our ability and conviction.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us, giving should not be done grudgingly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which we invite you to participate.
Not out of guilt.
Not out of fear.
Not because your salvation or God's favor can be purchased.
But because you may believe this ministry is worth helping to sustain.
These products can serve as reminders of Scripture, encouragement in daily life, and opportunities to share conversations about faith.
It is the opportunity to help keep biblical encouragement and discipleship resources reaching people who need them.
Pray for those struggling with sin.
Encourage someone who is trying to return to Christ.
Speak truth with gentleness.
Point people to the Bible.
And above all, point them to Jesus.
Because Gospel Warrior is not the Savior.
A ministry cannot forgive sin.
A Christian product cannot make anyone holy.
Only Jesus Christ saves.
Only His sacrifice is sufficient.
Only His resurrection secures the hope of eternal life.
And every faithful ministry must remain a servant of that Gospel, never a replacement for it.
So before you leave this article, return to the question one final time.
Can a genuine Christian live in unrepentant sin for years?
Do not use the uncertainty of another person's spiritual condition to avoid examining your own.
Do not use your struggles as a reason to despair.
And do not use God's patience as a reason to postpone repentance.
Instead, listen to the invitation of the One who gave His life for sinners.
Come to Him with your failures.
Come to Him with your pride.
Come to Him with the truth you have been hiding.
Come to Him without pretending that your chains are beautiful.
Because the cross is not a celebration of our rebellion.
It is the place where the holiness and love of God meet in the saving work of Jesus Christ.
And the empty tomb declares that sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
If you are ready, you can pray:

“Lord Jesus, I have spent too much time explaining away things I should have confessed. I have called some of my compromises harmless when Your Word has called me to repentance. Forgive me for the ways I have resisted Your truth. I cannot save myself, and I cannot transform my own heart through determination alone. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Teach me to trust You, to turn from what dishonors You, and to walk in the light. Give me courage to confess, wisdom to seek help, humility to accept correction, and strength through Your Spirit to follow You. Where I have harmed others, help me take responsibility. Where I have fallen, lead me back to Your grace. I do not want merely to look Christian. I want to belong to You and live for Your glory. In Your name, Jesus. Amen.”
And remember this when the screen goes dark, the room grows quiet, and you are alone again with the truth about your life.
The most dangerous place is not where your sin has brought you low, but where your heart has learned to call its chains freedom—while Jesus is still calling you into the light.
